records.current_summary:
Canada is exceptionally safe for trans visitors — the strongest of the large Western countries. Gender identity and expression are protected grounds in the Canadian Human Rights Act and the Criminal Code’s hate-crime provisions (Bill C-16, 2017); most provinces offer self-declaration legal gender recognition; federal documents offer an X marker; and healthcare coverage is universal. There are no bathroom laws, no border friction (Canadian authorities have not issued or received trans-traveller warnings), and courts consistently enforce protections.

The counterweights are real but climate-level: police-reported hate crimes have risen six consecutive years (+169% since 2018), with gender identity/expression crimes among the fastest-growing categories; Egale documents a rising organised anti-trans movement; and Alberta/Saskatchewan have enacted resident-facing policy rollbacks (school pronoun and healthcare restrictions). A 2022 federal survey found 39% of 2SLGBTQI+ respondents experienced identity-based violence in five years — 90% of it verbal abuse, 17% physical.

For a visitor: full legal protection, functioning recourse, low probability of anything beyond verbal harassment in hostile pockets; the current sources report no marriage or partner-travel friction.

prison_adds.title: LGBTQ people in prison — Canada section (Wikipedia)
prison_adds.summary: Placement policy: after Bill C-16 (2017) banned discrimination based on gender identity, transgender prisoners were to be placed in correctional facilities based on their gender identity, and Prime Minister Trudeau promised to review transgender prison assignment to ensure facilities match gender identity; transgender prisoners imprisoned for more than 12 continuous months are to be considered for sex-reassignment surgery. A 2022 study of Nova Scotia correctional officers found them generally mindful of trans-prisoner safety and security but with some concerns about risk to other prisoners; a 2022 CTV report alleged gender-diverse prisoners face a pattern of abuse and discrimination in Canadian jails and are more likely to be victims of sexual assault. No special-unit or solitary/segregation policy detail beyond the federal identity-based placement rule.

prison_adds.title: Barbara findlay (Wikipedia) — Synthia Kavanagh case
prison_adds.summary: Documented case: the article records that Canadian lawyer Barbara findlay represented Synthia Kavanagh, a transgender prisoner, in litigation concerning gender-affirming medical treatment and placement in a women's correctional institution — evidence that Canadian trans-prisoner placement and gender-affirming care were litigated in court. The Wikipedia article gives no dates or final outcome for the case, so this add is thin on specifics.

records.current_summary:
Switzerland is a very safe destination for transgender visitors. Legal gender recognition has worked by self-declaration since January 2022 — a personal declaration before the civil registrar, with no court or medical requirements (binary male/female only; no non-binary marker). Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2022 (approved by referendum), gender-neutral rape law took effect in 2024, and employers have a legal duty of care toward trans employees. General crime is exceptionally low.

The notable legislative shortcoming — flagged by the ILGA Rainbow Map and by the government's own review — is that the criminal hate-crime and hate-speech provision (Article 261bis) covers sexual orientation but not gender identity. So a person targeted specifically for being trans does not benefit from that aggravation in criminal law, though the protections available through employment and constitutional law are broader. Reported hate crimes against LGBTIQ people have risen about fivefold since 2020 (around six per week, but from a low absolute base of ~309 cases in 2024).

The federal government adopted Switzerland's first National Action Plan against LGBTIQ hate crime in January 2026 (running to 2030), signalling a pro-trans institutional direction. There is no rollback movement.

prison_adds.title: Gesetz über den Justizvollzug (Justizvollzugsgesetz, JVG) vom 13. November 2019 — Basel-Stadt detention law (TGNS)
prison_adds.summary: Primary legal text of the canton of Basel-Stadt's detention law (JVG, adopted 13 Nov 2019 by the Grand Council). §2 Trennungsvorschriften requires separation of female and male detainees and stipulates that 'the gender identity of the detained person is respected as far as possible' (Die Geschlechtsidentität der eingewiesenen Person wird soweit möglich beachtet); the prison directorate may deviate from the separation rules in consultation with the referring authority. This is the explicit 2019 inclusion of gender identity in a Swiss detention law aimed at protecting transgender people's placement in correctional facilities.

prison_adds.title: LGBTQ rights in Switzerland — placement of transgender people in correctional facilities (Wikipedia)
prison_adds.summary: Wikipedia overview of Swiss LGBTQ rights records that in November 2019 the Grand Council of Basel-Stadt voted to include 'gender identity' in its law on detention to better protect transgender people in regard to placement in correctional facilities, citing the TGNS-documented JVG. No national (federal) trans-prisoner placement rule is documented in the article — placement practice is cantonal; no Swiss case law, special trans units or federal solitary-confinement practice for trans prisoners are noted.

records.current_summary:
Côte d'Ivoire is dangerous for trans visitors — a sharp recent deterioration. Same-sex conduct has never been criminalised, but in late 2024 the country saw a wave of violence: social-media influencers exhorted followers to 'hunt' gay and gender-nonconforming people, and dozens of assaults and beatings followed. There is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection, and police response to the hunt wave was inadequate.

For a visitor: no statutory exposure, but the 2024 hunt-down campaign makes visible gender nonconformity dangerous, especially in the largest city (Abidjan).

prison_adds.title: Côte d'Ivoire | Country Page — Human Rights Watch
prison_adds.summary: Thin: no usable prison-housing finding. HRW's Côte d'Ivoire country page contains no document, case or report on transgender prisoners: 'LGBT Rights' appears only as a topic-facet link, and no HRW publication is listed on where trans detainees are housed (birth-sex vs identity placement), special units, or solitary/segregation practice in Ivorian prisons.

records.current_summary:
Costa Rica is workable for trans visitors — Central America's strongest jurisdiction by a wide margin. Same-sex relations have been legal since 1971; marriage equality arrived in 2020 via the Inter-American Court's Advisory Opinion 24/2017 (which also established the right to legal gender recognition across the region); and trans people can change their name and photo on ID documents administratively. Institutions function: an ombudsman, a constitutional chamber (Sala IV) with a long pro-equality record, and universal healthcare that covers transition-related care.

Counterweights are modest: the Catholic Church is the official religion and culturally influential; the ID process changes name and photo but not the sex marker itself; and anti-discrimination enforcement is uneven. There is no bathroom debate of consequence, no police targeting, and tourist infrastructure is accustomed to diverse visitors. San José has a visible scene.

prison_adds.title: Transexuales reclusos en carceles nacionales podran optar entre prision de hombres o mujeres (AmeliaRueda.com)
prison_adds.summary: AmeliaRueda.com (Alonso Mata Blanco, 25 Jun 2017): Costa Rica's Justice Ministry (Vice-Minister Marco Feoli) announced that prisoners who self-identify as transsexual may choose whether to serve their sentence in a men's or a women's facility - relocation to the facility matching gender identity, strictly voluntary, decided case-by-case with prison social workers and psychologists; a circular ordered a census of self-identified trans prisoners, an exclusive module for trans people was under consideration, and Spain's system was cited as the model (protocols for vulnerable prison populations developed with CEJIL since 2016). Official policy-level documentation of placement-by-gender-identity in the regional context.

prison_adds.title: Stephanie, la transgenero que vive en la carcel rodeada de hombres | CR Hoy
prison_adds.summary: CRHoy (Javier Paniagua, 22 Jun 2019): Stephanie, a trans woman serving ~6 years for drug-trafficking complicity, is held at CAI Orosi de Cartago - a men's facility ('en esa sede solo hay hombres'); she transitioned while incarcerated and says prison offers 'solo hay dos opciones: o sos hombre o mujer aqui'. The Justice Ministry told CRHoy there were 23 transgender people in the national system at the time. Stephanie recounts identity-targeted abuse including a broomstick-handle rape at La Reforma (Alajuela) witnessed by a custodian. Shows that despite the 2017 choice policy, trans women were still found in men's facilities in 2019 and faced violence with custodial inaction.

records.current_summary:
Ecuador is a country that demands real caution from trans visitors. Legal gender recognition has existed since 2016, and the legal framework is now among the region's strongest. The 2024 reform lets adults change name and sex/gender on the identity document directly through the civil registry (one time, no surgery), and in 2024-25 court rulings extended document changes to trans adolescents and reprimanded the legislature for stalling trans-rights implementation.

The violence side is severe: a monitoring group documented 27 LGBTQ+ people murdered in 2023 with inadequate state response, and the "internal armed conflict" against gangs has intensified general violence since January 2024, with two more LGBTQ people killed in its first weeks; Quito and Guayaquil, the two main cities, carry real street risk, and police capacity is consumed by the security crisis.

For a visitor: documents and expression are legally protected, but the probability of encountering violence if outed in public is among the highest in the region right now.

prison_adds.title: Trans Women in Ecuador's Prisons | PrisioTrans Human Rights Program
prison_adds.summary: Silueta X (leading Ecuadorian trans-rights organisation), PrisioTrans program, documents 2011-2026: trans women in Ecuador's almost universally male prisons are held in male spaces and face gender-identity discrimination, unsafe placement, sexual violence, forced suppression of gender expression and health-care barriers. Key cases: trans woman Helen Maldonado died during the November 2021 massacre at Penitenciaria del Litoral while held in a male prison space; 2022 complaint over cruel/inhuman/degrading treatment of trans women in Lago Agrio; 2024 allegations of forced head-shaving, beatings and violence targeting breast/body implants; 2026 death in State custody of a 23-year-old trans woman drew calls for an independent investigation at the El Encuentro maximum-security prison. The program explicitly does NOT push a one-size placement rule, instead advocating individualised housing decisions per Inter-American standards considering gender identity, safety, the detainee's own assessment and informed consent, and cites the July 2016 government decision to develop protocols for LGBT people deprived of liberty.

prison_adds.title: Trans Women Report Being Punished for Their Identity in Ecuador Prisons (Spanish)
prison_adds.summary: Pulitzer Center investigation: Ecuador's prisons are 'almost always male' - the last prison census counted 73 trans women across all Ecuadorian prisons (organisation Fundacion Vivir Libre says there are many more), and trans women are placed in male pavilions. Case: Venezuelan trans woman Alexa (27) detained Aug 2023 at Penitenciaria del Litoral was initially sent to male pavilion 9 with three other trans women rather than the 'prioritaria' pavilion reserved for vulnerable populations (where many sexo-gender-diverse inmates are held); she received no medical exams or HIV treatment there. The story documents rapes and torture reported to be directed at prisoners' gender identity, showing placement practice operates by birth sex/legal sex with protective 'prioritaria' placement used unevenly.
